meta.title: GeoAI in Practice: Evaluating a Unified Open-Source Library for Geospatial AI
meta.authorsHtml: Adriano Gentile<sup>1</sup>, Claudio Domenico Giuliani<sup>1</sup>, Antonio Maci<sup>∗</sup><sup>1,3</sup>, Pietro Sangermano<sup>1</sup>, Alessandro Santorsola<sup>1,2</sup>

abstract: The proliferation of machine learning applications in geospatial analysis has resulted in a fragmented ecosystem of Python libraries, each covering specific workflow aspects without offering a unified interface. This fragmentation increases implementation complexity and steepens the learning curve for researchers and practitioners. We evaluate GeoAI, an open-source Python library designed to integrate artificial intelligence methods with geospatial workflows, against TorchGeo and TerraTorch on two fundamental tasks: land cover classification and building footprint extraction. A controlled experimental setup enforces identical data, model configurations, and functional specifications across frameworks. The toolchain fragmentation is quantified by aggregating the static structural metrics into a composite fragmentation index. GeoAI reduces code volume by over 80% and achieves comparable reductions in structural fragmentation across both tasks, reflecting systematic architectural compactness.

blocks.html: Open source geospatial tools have evolved from niche utilities to foundational infrastructure, enabling unprecedented accessibility in spatial analysis. This shift from fragmented proprietary systems to collaborative, community-driven platforms paved the way for scalable, inclusive innovation in diverse fields [1]. Openness in geospatial software and data rooted in community participation evolved from initial skepticism to institutional adoption for flagship initiatives, enabling a new paradigm where dynamic frameworks for collaborative analysis transcend static tool cataloging [2]. This evolution is particularly impactful in spatial analysis, fostering the rapid development of novel methodologies and facilitating data-driven decision-making across disciplines [3]. Recent advances in machine learning (ML), as a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI), have dramatically boosted the capabilities of open source geospatial data analysis, providing access to models capable of extracting meaningful insights from complex spatial data patterns [4]. Built on the foundations of deep learning (DL) and natural language processing (NLP), the current escalation in generative AI technologies is poised to revolutionize geospatial data analysis. These advances promise increasingly sophisticated tools capable of generalizing across diverse datasets and supporting complex, data-driven decisions in space-related mission operations [5, 6]. Specifically, recent work explored the synergistic potential of large language models (LLMs) to support human analysts in Earth observation tasks [7, 8], while also investigating the integration of generative AI within established geospatial ecosystems to unlock new capabilities and enhance existing workflows [9]. As a direct result, and being Python the widely adopted programming language within the ML community, a vibrant ecosystem of Python-based libraries has been rapidly developed to support such applications. This has reduced the entry barriers for researchers and practitioners alike [10]. Two of the commonly used Python libraries for these tasks are:

• TorchGeo [11], which is a PyTorch-based [12] library for DL with geospatial data. It provides standardized datasets, data loaders, samplers, and pretrained models tailored for remote sensing tasks, such as land cover classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. It simplifies training and evaluation pipelines for Earth observation imagery within the PyTorch ecosystem. However, more sophisticated use cases may require a deeper knowledge of PyTorch and external tools for full ML workflow orchestration.

• TerraTorch [13] is an open-source Python library built on PyTorch and its Lightning version for scalable geospatial DL. Provided by IBM, it represents an efficient toolkit for fine-tuning pretrained models. However, it may result too complex for small projects due to the heavier abstraction layer and being primarily DL-centric, focusing less on traditional geographic information system (GIS) workflows.

A recent study by Adam J. Stewart et al. [14] provides a comprehensive qualitative overview of a variety of ML Python libraries for geospatial data analysis and explicitly identifies fragmentation as a limiting factor. Although orch- Geo, and TerraTorch offer strong foundational capabilities for geospatial DL, there is still a need for more comprehensive, high-level interfaces that can make advanced AI methods accessible to the wider geospatial community. GeoAI [15] is designed to bridge this gap by simplifying the interaction between AI frameworks and geospatial data workflows. Instead of requiring users to coordinate multiple tools and libraries manually, a cohesive and accessible layer that streamlines the entire process is provided. This approach benefits several audiences: geospatial scientists who want to incorporate AI methods without deep expertise in ML; AI specialists who need efficient access to geospatial preprocessing tools and curated datasets; and instructors who require clear and reproducible workflows suitable for teaching. At its core, GeoAI prioritizes usability while retaining analytical depth. Complex applications, such as extracting building footprints from satellite imagery, performing land cover mapping, or conducting change detection analyses, can be implemented with minimal code. By combining modern AI models, e.g. interfaces to the most well-known generative AI providers, with straightforward access to widely used geospatial data sources, the framework reduces technical overhead while still supporting advanced experimentation and research-level customization. This work presents a comparative analysis between the GeoAI framework and state-of-the-art solutions, providing a snapshot of their implementation and structural complexity in geospatial data analysis projects, and introducing objective metrics to systematically assess their impact on software development practices in both academic research and industrial open-source contexts.

This chapter evaluates to what extent and in what ways GeoAI reduces toolchain fragmentation compared to alternative state-of-the-art frameworks. To answer such a research question, a controlled comparative setup that ensures even conditions in tasks, data, computational environment, and model configuration is established. Then, quantitative metrics that capture the implementation and setup-to-result complexities are defined.

blocks.title: Methodological setup of the comparative analysis

blocks.html: This section describes the experimental design adopted to comparatively assess toolchain fragmentation across different geospatial analysis frameworks. The evaluation focuses on structural and integration complexity rather than predictive performance. To ensure methodological consistency, all frameworks are evaluated on identical functional objectives under controlled I/O specifications. The comparative setup comprises the following points:
• The identification of competitors according to the
statement of need in [15], as recalled in the section 1, resulting in TorchGeo and TerraTorch being selected.

• Two widely addressed tasks on geospatial data were selected: land cover classification and building footprint extraction. Both tasks are commonly addressed across geospatial ML toolchains and can be implemented independently of a specific framework abstraction. Land cover classification involves assigning a semantic label to each pixel of a remotely sensed raster image to produce a categorical land cover map.

This task represents a canonical supervised raster-based workflow and exercises the full data-processing pipeline, including raster I/O, preprocessing, model training, and spatially explicit inference. For this task, the comparative evaluation was conducted between GeoAI and TorchGeo. Building footprint extraction is formulated as the delineation of building geometries from remotely sensed imagery. Operationally, this typically involves semantic segmentation followed by raster-to-vector conversion and geometric postprocessing. Therefore, the task stresses not only the model inference, but also the spatial transformation and integration steps within the toolchain. For this task, the benchmark between GeoAI and TerraTorch was performed.

• To ensure methodological consistency across frameworks, the comparative analysis enforced a uniform functional contract: identical input data formats, equivalent preprocessing assumptions, and consistent output specifications for each task. These specifications were derived based on the use case examples provided in the API reference of GeoAI<sup>1</sup>. The data employed in both cases were downloaded from Hugging Face GeoAI’s author repository<sup>2345</sup>. Where model-based training was involved, equivalent architectural configurations and hyperparameter settings were adopted. This design isolates structural and toolchain-related differences from variations in predictive performance. Finally, the experiments were performed using the following hardware settings:
AMD EPYC 7252 8-core processor 3.1 GHz CPU, one NVIDIA A30 24 GB GPU, and 100 GB RAM (DDR4 3200 MHz).

The external dependency dispersion, ˜Dext (β3 = 0.2), quantifies the toolchain fragmentation import level. For the Footprint task, GeoAI reduces the required code volume by approximately 88% compared to TerraTorch, while FI decreases by over 90%. This indicates that most of the code in excess corresponds to the integration and orchestration layers rather than the modeling logic. A comparable trend emerges in the land cover experiment, where GeoAI achieves nearly 80% reduction in Lcode and roughly 75% decrease in the fragmentation index relative to TorchGeo. Averaged across tasks, the overall contraction exceeds 80% both in terms of code footprint and structural fragmentation. The consistency across independent tasks suggests that the reduction is not task-specific but reflects the systematic simplification of a toolchain architecture. Importantly, as illustrated in figure 2, the GeoAI configurations consistently occupy the low-fragmentation region of the normalized landscape, reinforcing the argument that the observed gains are derived from architectural compactness rather than isolated implementation choices.

blocks.html: The results indicate a consistent relationship between the streamlined framework architecture and the reduced integration effort. A smaller codebase and fewer declared dependencies typically mean fewer coordination points between libraries, less boilerplate, and a reduced surface for incompatibilities. This can translate into faster onboarding in practice because new contributors navigate a shallower abstraction stack. It also reduces the exposure to version conflicts and the probability of silent failures caused by loosely coupled components. From a maintenance perspective, a compact pipeline is easier to refactor, test, and evolve. However, highly integrated frameworks tend to impose stronger design assumptions. Although this reduces orchestration overhead, it may limit flexibility in edge cases where each component requires fine-grained control. In contrast, more modular toolchains can be advantageous in exploratory scenarios where heterogeneous components must be combined in unconventional ways. For this reason, the goal of the fragmentation index is not to rank frameworks universally, but rather to make structural overhead measurable. The appropriate balance between compactness and modularity ultimately depends on the intended use case. This study remains intentionally scoped. First, two representative tasks for each dataset were tested. Although they cover common GeoAI workflows, broader empirical validation would require additional tasks and data regimes. Second, the proposed metrics are structural and static. Lines of code and dependency dispersion provide insight into integration effort, but they do not capture runtime indicators or qualitative aspects of code readability. Finally, the experiments were conducted in a controlled research setting. While structural simplicity is often correlated with ease of maintenance, this assumption should be validated in real-world production pipelines. Future extensions will include additional tasks, a larger set of competing tools, and dynamic factors such as setup time and maintenance cost. Longitudinal measurements, including the impact of dependency updates over time, would further clarify the overall sustainability of ecosystem.
